title: The Letter You Didn't Send

post.author: u/night_treasurer_azadeh
post.title: I'm the volunteer treasurer of a small charity. Tonight I found £8,640 paid to a stranger on our director's word. She says she never wrote it.

blocks.text: I'm Azadeh, volunteer treasurer of the Wickstead Trust, a small charity that pays for home repairs for older people. Once a month, at night, I check every payment our bank made against our own list. That check is a reconciliation.

Tonight, Thursday 1 October, I reconciled September: 46 payments. We keep a supplier file, a list of each supplier's bank details and phone number. Forty-five went to accounts in it. One didn't: £8,640 to Harcastle Heating for invoice 1187, paid on Thursday 24 September to an account I'd never seen.

Mr Tuckwell, our part-time bookkeeper, pays suppliers alone once our director, Ms Kilbride, approves by email. Their thread is in the finance mailbox. Each line shows the date and time, who the message says it's from, the part of the address after the @, and what it asked, in general words:

14 Sep 09:12  Mr Tuckwell    ours        invoice 1187, £8,640: please approve (Harcastle copied in)
15 Sep 08:47  Ms Kilbride    ours        approved
22 Sep 10:31  "Ms Kilbride"  lookalike   asks that invoice 1187 go to a new account
24 Sep 14:05  our bank       the bank's  payment sent: £8,640 to the new account

The part after the @ is the domain: the name of whoever the mail claims to come from. On 22 September it was our charity's name with one letter changed. A name made to pass for a trusted one is a lookalike domain. A public lookup shows it was first registered on Thursday 17 September, three days after the thread began.
The reply ended with Ms Kilbride's usual sign-off, name, title and phone, copied exactly. At 23:52 I texted her. At 00:05 she answered: she never wrote it.
Her name, in her words, at the foot of a letter she never sent.

An email that pretends to come from someone you trust, to make you act, is phishing. One aimed at a named person, using real details like our thread, is spear-phishing. It works because the reader sees a familiar name in a conversation they already trust.

Mr Tuckwell's mail program had marked the reply as passing three checks. A domain can publish a list of its mail servers, the computers allowed to send its mail. A receiving server compares where a message came from with that list. That check is SPF, short for Sender Policy Framework.

A domain can also seal each message, like wax on a letter, with a secret only it holds. Anyone can test the seal with a key the domain publishes; if the message changed on the way, the seal breaks. That's DKIM, short for DomainKeys Identified Mail.

The third, DMARC, short for Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting and Conformance, checks that SPF or DKIM passed for the same domain you see after the @. It also lets a domain say what to do with mail that fails: deliver it, put it with the junk, or reject it, which bounces it back.

blocks.label: september_thread_and_payment.png

diagram.aria: My sketch of September. Top row: the real thread on 14 and 15 September, from our own domain; the lookalike domain, first registered on 17 September; and the forged reply on 22 September at 10:31, which passed SPF, DKIM and DMARC. Bottom row: the supplier file, holding Harcastle's account since 4 March 2019; the payment of £8,640 on 24 September at 14:05 to an account that differs from the file; and September's 46 payments, one of them to an account not on file.

notes.text: 45 of 46 went to accounts on file

blocks.caption: Redrawn from my notes on 1 October 2026. The real thread ran on 14 and 15 September from our own domain. The lookalike was first registered on 17 September, and the forged reply came from it on 22 September at 10:31, passing all three checks. On 24 September at 14:05, £8,640 went to an account that is not Harcastle's in our supplier file, where its details have sat since 4 March 2019: 1 of September's 46 payments.

blocks.text: Our domain publishes none of the three. The lookalike publishes all three, and passed all three, for itself.

At 00:30 I rang our bank's fraud line. They'll ask the receiving bank to recall the money, send it back, but money that left a week ago is often gone. Ms Kilbride wants a new rule before October's payments. What should we change?

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: Look at the dates before you choose, Azadeh. The lookalike appeared three days after the thread began, and the reply knew the invoice number. Who else could read that thread? Then the account: where else is Harcastle's written down, and who besides Mr Tuckwell sees a payment before it leaves? One word for your notes: the name your mail program shows in bold beside an address is the display name. Anyone can type any display name.

replies.author: u/night_treasurer_azadeh
replies.text: Harcastle's accounts address was copied in from the first message. Their account and office number have been in our supplier file since Monday 4 March 2019. And nobody else sees a payment: Mr Tuckwell pays alone, so suppliers never wait. Harcastle's invoice isn't due yet, so they haven't chased the money.

comments.author: u/reject_policy_pettigrew
comments.text: This is a solved problem. Faking the sender of an email is called spoofing, and DMARC set to reject solves spoofing; our IT firm said so. Publish SPF, DKIM and DMARC for your domain, set the policy to reject, and forged mail from your director bounces before anyone reads it. Phone calls and extra sign-offs are what you do when your email is broken. Fix the email.

replies.author: u/night_treasurer_azadeh
replies.text: Ms Kilbride likes this one. It costs nothing and asks nothing of the staff.

comments.author: u/red_banner_mountjoy
comments.text: Two cheap things worked at my last office. Every email from outside our domain arrived with a red banner across the top saying so. And IT ran a phishing test each month: a harmless practice email, sent with management's agreement, to see who clicks its link. Anyone who clicked redid the training. People got careful fast.

reply.prompt: The October payments start on Monday 5 October. What should the Wickstead Trust change? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Turn on the email checks SPF, DKIM and DMARC, so forged mail from the director bounces.
options.part2: A volunteer published SPF, DKIM and DMARC for our domain, with the policy set to reject. In the sim, sample 8, a message claiming our exact address from servers we don't list, now bounces, and our own mail passes: 11 of the 12 samples pass all three. But sample 6, the lookalike, passes all three for its own domain, just as the reply did on 22 September. Replaying September, £8,640 still goes to the new account: 45 of 46 payments to accounts on file. Our checks protect our name; the lookalike never used it. On Friday 9 October the bank wrote: the receiving account was emptied on Friday 25 September, and nothing came back.
options.senior: Publish SPF, DKIM and DMARC for your own domain: it stops exact forgeries of your address and tells you who sends mail in your name. But all three check the domain the message actually shows, and a lookalike domain is a different domain with its own valid records. RFC 9989 says it plainly: DMARC does not address visually similar domain names or display names. Checks prove where mail came from, not whether the request is real; the payment needs its own check.

options.text: Show a red warning banner on every email that comes from outside the charity's domain.
options.part2: We switched on a banner for outside mail. In the sim it sits on 9 of the 12 samples, and in September it would have marked 287 of the 312 emails in the finance mailbox, the forged reply among them. Most of a charity's mail comes from outside: donors, suppliers, the bank. Mr Tuckwell says that by the second week he no longer saw it. Replaying September, £8,640 still goes to the new account. The banner goes by the address after the @, so it also misses sample 8, which claims our own. On Friday 9 October the bank wrote: the receiving account was emptied on Friday 25 September, and nothing came back.
options.senior: Outside-sender banners are cheap and worth having, but a warning on nearly every message stops carrying information, and people learn to skip it. A banner can't tell a lookalike from a real supplier, and it can't confirm a request. Use it as one layer, and keep the control that matters at the point where money moves: verify any change of payment details through a channel the request didn't give you.

options.text: Confirm any change of bank details by phoning a number on file, before paying.
options.part2: Ms Kilbride signed the rule on Saturday 3 October: any change to a payee's bank details, whoever asks and however the request arrives, waits until someone rings the payee on the number already in our supplier file, never a number from the request. In the sim, replaying September with the call back on: on Thursday 24 September Mr Tuckwell rings Harcastle on its office number, on file since Monday 4 March 2019. Harcastle's bank hasn't changed. £8,640 goes to the account on file: 46 of 46 payments to accounts on file, £0 to a new one. The call takes minutes and needs nothing from our email. On Friday 9 October the bank wrote: the receiving account was emptied on Friday 25 September, and nothing came back. September's money is gone; October's is not.
options.senior: Business email compromise wins by changing where money goes, so put the check on that change, through a channel the attacker doesn't control. A call back on a number you already held proves the request with the real person; a number in the request proves nothing. It works however good the forgery is, whatever the domain, display name or checks say. Pair it with a second person on every payment, keep SPF, DKIM and DMARC for your own domain, and teach staff that reporting a strange request is always welcome.

options.text: Send all staff a phishing test each month, and retrain anyone who clicks on the link.
options.part2: A monthly link test is not a setting in the sim, because it changes no number: the forged reply had no link to click. It asked a trusted person to do a normal task, paying an invoice, to a new account. Replaying September, £8,640 still goes to the new account. In October two staff clicked the practice link and were sent back to training; one later told Ms Kilbride she would rather say nothing about an odd email than be the name on the next list. On Friday 9 October the bank wrote: the receiving account was emptied on Friday 25 September, and nothing came back.
options.senior: Phishing simulations can help, if they are run fairly: written scope agreed by leadership, staff told a programme exists, safe and easy reporting, results used to improve training, never to shame. But a click rate measures links, and this attack had none. Retraining as punishment teaches people to hide mistakes, and the defender needs the opposite: fast reports. Train for the request that matters, a change of payment details, and make the process verify it.

sim.title: Spot the samples, then replay September's payment
sim.lede: You're Azadeh, before Monday 14 September 2026. As given data: 12 training samples, each a short description in general words, never real email text, 6 of them worth checking before acting. Our domain is shown as wicksteadtrust.example; .example is a reserved ending no one can register. The lookalike's sixth letter differs, and the sim shows it only as a question mark. September: 46 payments; invoice 1187, £8,640 to Harcastle Heating; Harcastle's account and number in the supplier file since Monday 4 March 2019; the finance mailbox got 312 emails, 287 from outside our domain. Read each sample's checks and sender's domain beside ours, letter by letter, and mark it. Then choose the defences: SPF, DKIM and DMARC for our domain with the policy set to reject; a banner on outside mail; a call back to the payee on the number on file before any change of bank details; two people for every payment, where the second compares the account with the supplier file. Play September and read where £8,640 goes.
sim.tryThis: Try this: pick sample 6. Letter 6 of 22 differs, and SPF, DKIM and DMARC all pass for its own domain. Play September as built: 45 of 46 payments to accounts on file, £8,640 to the new account. Turn our checks on: 11 samples pass all three, sample 8 bounces, and £8,640 still goes. Swap to the banner: it sits on 9 of 12 samples and 287 of 312 emails, and £8,640 still goes. Turn on the call back: 46 of 46, £0. Try two people instead: held, £0.

explain.oneLine: Nobody broke into the charity's email. A stranger set up a domain one letter away from the charity's, replied in a real thread under the director's name, and passed every email check for its own domain. The money moved because one person could change where it went on the strength of an email. Check any change of bank details by phone on a number already on file, and put two people on every payment.

steps.title: What happened: business email compromise.
steps.text: Business email compromise is a fraud that uses work email to get money paid to the wrong place. Here it went in four steps. First, someone learned of a real invoice thread; Harcastle's address was copied in, and how the stranger read it is not known tonight. Second, they registered a domain with one letter changed, on 17 September. Third, they replied in the thread under the director's display name, asking for a new account. Fourth, one person paid it. What goes wrong at each step: a thread shared outside the charity, a name nobody compares letter by letter, a display name anyone can type, and a payment nobody else sees.

steps.title: What SPF, DKIM and DMARC prove, and what they don't.
steps.text: When mail arrives, the receiving server runs three checks. First, SPF: it looks up the sender domain's published list and asks whether the sending server is on it. Second, DKIM: it fetches the domain's published key and tests the seal, which proves the sealed parts weren't changed on the way. Third, DMARC: it checks that SPF or DKIM passed for the domain shown after the @, and applies that domain's policy: deliver, junk, or reject. Together they prove the message came from servers the named domain allows, unchanged. They don't prove the domain is the one you think, who typed the message, or that the request is genuine. The lookalike owns its domain, so it passed all three.

steps.title: Verify the change, not the email.
steps.text: The control belongs where the money changes direction. First, treat any request to change a payee's bank details as unconfirmed, however it arrives. Second, look up the payee's phone number in your own records, the number on file, never one from the request. Third, ring and ask whether the details changed. Fourth, only then update the file and pay. What goes wrong: a number taken from the request reaches the fraudster; a rule with exceptions for urgent or senior requests is the rule an attacker aims at.

steps.title: Two people for every payment.
steps.text: Splitting a task so no one person can finish it alone is called separation of duties. For payments: one person sets up the payment, a second approves it in the bank's system after comparing the account with the supplier file. A change of account then needs two people fooled, not one. What goes wrong: a second person who approves without looking, or one who sees only the same forged email, adds a signature and no check.

steps.title: Running phishing simulations fairly.
steps.text: A phishing simulation sends staff harmless practice messages to measure and teach. Run it in steps. First, written scope, agreed by leadership: what is sent, to whom, when, and what is never imitated. Second, consent at the organisation level and staff told that a programme exists. Third, a safe, one-click way to report anything odd, real or practice, and thanks for every report. Fourth, results used to improve training and processes, never to name or shame. Practice should include requests with no link at all, like a change of bank details, because that is what reached Mr Tuckwell.

diagram.aria: The fix, drawn for invoice 1187. A request to change a payee's bank details, from any sender and any channel, pauses for a call back on the number on file, Harcastle's since 2019. If the call confirms, the second person compares the account with the supplier file and approves, and £8,640 goes to the account on file. If the call doesn't confirm, the payment is held.

explain.caption: The fix, drawn for invoice 1187. Any request to change bank details pauses for a call back on the number already on file. If Harcastle confirms, the second person compares the account with the supplier file and approves; £8,640 goes to the account on file. If not, the payment is held.

fix.title: The fix: verify every change of bank details by phone on a number on file, and two people on every payment
fix.text: Write one rule and let nobody waive it: any change to a payee's bank details, from anyone, by any channel, waits until someone rings the payee on the number already in the supplier file and the payee confirms. Record who rang, when, and what was said. Then put two people on every payment: one sets it up, a second approves it in the bank's system after comparing the account with the supplier file. Keep SPF, DKIM and DMARC published for the charity's own domain with a reject policy, so exact forgeries of its address bounce. Keep invoice threads inside the charity where you can. Run an awareness programme that teaches this one request by name, with a one-click way to report and thanks for every report. Ask the bank about its own checks on new payees, and report any loss to the bank and the police at once, because a recall only works while the money is still there.

limits: A call back only works on a number you already trusted. If the supplier file itself can be changed by one person on the word of an email or a letter, the attacker changes the number first; changes to the file need the same check and a second person.

Two people can both be fooled, especially if the second sees only the same forged email or approves without looking. The second check has to look at something the attacker didn't send: the supplier file.
None of this recovers September's money. A recall depends on the receiving bank and how fast the loss is reported; money moved on within a day is often gone.

explain.seniorTake: Email authentication answers one question, did this message come from servers the named domain allows, unchanged, and business email compromise is built to pass it: the attacker uses a domain they own, a display name anyone can type, or a real mailbox they've broken into. So the defence can't live only in the inbox. Put the control where money changes direction: any change of payment details is verified through a channel the request didn't supply, a call back on a number already on file, and every payment needs a second person who checks the record, not the email. Publish SPF, DKIM and DMARC for your own domain anyway, with a reject policy once your own mail passes, because exact forgeries of your name are real and the reports show who sends as you. Run awareness as a programme, not a trap: written scope, consent, practice that includes requests with no link, a one-click way to report, and no shaming, because the defender's best signal is a fast report from someone who isn't afraid to make one.

realWorld.title: Ubiquiti, 2015: $46.7 million by impersonation
realWorld.text: Ubiquiti's Form 8-K of August 2015 says: "On June 5, 2015, the Company determined that it had been the victim of a criminal fraud." It describes "employee impersonation and fraudulent requests from an outside entity", which "resulted in transfers of funds aggregating $46.7 million held by a Company subsidiary". Of that, "the Company has recovered $8.1 million of the amounts transferred", with a further $6.8 million then under legal injunction. The filing also says: "The Company has implemented enhanced internal controls over financial reporting since June 5, 2015".

realWorld.title: Rimasauskas: posing as a supplier
realWorld.text: A Lithuanian man posed as a large Asian hardware supplier, using email accounts made to look like its staff, and two US internet companies wired him money. SecurityAffairs, reporting the US Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York in December 2019, quotes the US Attorney: "Evaldas Rimasauskas devised an audacious scheme to fleece U.S. companies out of more than $120m,". He was sentenced to five years in prison. We could not read the Justice Department's own release page; its address is listed in the sources.

realWorld.title: RFC 9989 (DMARC, May 2026): what a pass means
realWorld.text: The current DMARC specification, which obsoletes RFC 7489, says: "A DMARC pass for a message indicates only that the use of the Author Domain has been validated for that message". And on lookalikes: "DMARC does not attempt to solve all problems with spoofed or otherwise fraudulent emails." In particular, "it does not address the use of visually similar domain names". Its out-of-scope list includes "Attacks in the display name portions of the RFC5322.From header field".

realWorld.title: SPF: which servers may send
realWorld.text: SPF's specification, RFC 7208, says domain owners "can explicitly authorize the hosts that are allowed to use their domain names". It is a list of permitted senders for one domain; it says nothing about whether that domain is the one the reader expects.

realWorld.title: DKIM: a seal of responsibility
realWorld.text: DKIM's specification, RFC 6376, says it "permits a person, role, or organization that owns the signing domain to claim some responsibility for a message", and "Assertion of responsibility is validated through a cryptographic signature". The owner of a lookalike domain can claim responsibility for its own mail just as validly.

realWorld.title: NIST SP 800-50 Rev. 1: a learning programme, not a test
realWorld.text: NIST's Building a Cybersecurity and Privacy Learning Program (September 2024) describes a programme "that manages awareness, training, and education programs for a diverse set of federal employee audiences." It says "The program should encourage behavior change as part of risk management and lead to developing a privacy" and security culture, and that it "includes suggested metrics and evaluation methods". Behaviour change and culture, not a click count.

asked: What do SPF, DKIM and DMARC each prove?
How do you stop business email compromise?
How would you run a phishing simulation fairly?
interview.answer: SPF lets a domain publish which servers may send its mail; a receiver checks the sending server against that list. DKIM has the sending domain seal the message with a secret key; a receiver tests the seal with the key the domain publishes, which shows the sealed parts weren't changed and that the domain took responsibility. DMARC ties those to the domain shown after the @, says what to do with failures, deliver, junk or reject, and sends reports to the domain owner. Together they prove a message came from servers the named domain allows, unchanged. They don't prove the domain is the one you think, the display name is true, or the request is genuine: a lookalike domain passes all three for itself, and a broken-into real mailbox passes for the real domain. So to stop business email compromise, I'd put the control on the money, not the inbox. Any change of payment details is verified by phone on a number already on file, never one from the request, with no exceptions for urgent or senior requests. Every payment needs two people, the second checking the account against the supplier record. Changes to supplier records get the same check. Publish SPF, DKIM and DMARC for your own domains with a reject policy once your own mail passes, and read the reports. For a phishing simulation: written scope agreed by leadership, organisational consent and staff told that a programme exists, scenarios that include no-link requests like bank-detail changes, a one-click report button, thanks for every report, results used to fix training and processes, and nobody named or shamed. I'd measure reporting rate and time to report, not only clicks. I'd close with the charity: every check passed, one letter differed, and one call on a number on file since 2019 would have kept £8,640.

terms.def: The small charity in this story, which pays for home repairs for older people. Azadeh is its volunteer treasurer; Ms Kilbride its director; Mr Tuckwell its part-time bookkeeper.
Checking every payment the bank made against your own list of what should have been paid, to find anything that doesn't match. Azadeh does it once a month.
The charity's own list of each supplier's bank details and phone number. Harcastle's have been in it since Monday 4 March 2019.
The part of an email address after the @: the name of the organisation the mail claims to come from. Like the street name on a return address.
A domain made to pass for a trusted one, here the charity's name with one letter changed. It is a different domain, with its own owner and its own email checks.
The name a mail program shows beside an address, often in bold. The sender types it, so it can say anything.
An email (or other message) that pretends to come from someone you trust, to make you act: click, sign in, or pay.
Phishing aimed at one named person, using real details such as a live thread or an invoice number, so it reads as ordinary work.
Fraud that uses work email, forged or broken into, to get money paid to the wrong place, often by changing a supplier's bank details.
Faking the sender of an email, such as putting someone else's exact address in the From line.
A computer that sends or receives email for a domain. The receiving server is the one that runs the checks on arriving mail.
Sender Policy Framework: a domain publishes which mail servers may send its mail, and a receiver checks the sending server against that list. RFC 7208.
DomainKeys Identified Mail: the sending domain seals each message with a secret key; a receiver tests the seal with a key the domain publishes. A pass shows the sealed parts were not changed.
Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting and Conformance: checks SPF or DKIM passed for the domain shown after the @, and applies that domain's policy. RFC 9989.
What a domain asks receivers to do with mail that fails DMARC: deliver it, put it with the junk, or reject it.
When a receiving server refuses a message and sends notice of it back to the sender, so it never reaches the inbox.
A warning a mail system adds to messages from other domains. Cheap, but on most of a small office's mail it soon goes unread.
Checking a request by phoning the person on a number you already held, never one given in the request.
A phone number already in your own records before any request came, such as Harcastle's office number in the supplier file.
Splitting a task so no one person can finish it alone, such as one person setting up a payment and a second approving it.
Harmless practice messages sent to staff, with leadership's written agreement, to teach and measure. Also called a phishing test.
The agreed document for a simulation: what is sent, to whom, when, what is never imitated, and how results are used.
Ongoing teaching that helps staff notice and report risks, measured by behaviour such as reports, not only by clicks.
Asking the receiving bank to send a payment back. It depends on the money still being in the account.
This case's plain word for DKIM's cryptographic signature on a message, tested with the domain's published key.
Request for Comments: the numbered documents in which the internet's standards are published, such as RFC 9989 for DMARC.
An international standard for running information security. Annex A 6.3 covers awareness, education and training; A.5.14 information transfer.
An audit report, written by an outside checker, on a company's controls against the AICPA's Trust Services Criteria. CC2.2 covers communicating security duties internally.
US NIST guidance, September 2024, on building a cybersecurity and privacy learning programme: awareness, training and education.

atWork: Find every place where one person can change where money goes on the strength of a message: a supplier's "new bank details" by email is a common pattern, and so is an urgent request that seems to come from a director. For each, ask three things. Is every change of payment details confirmed by phone on a number already on file, never one from the request, with no exceptions for urgency or seniority? Does every payment, and every change to the supplier records, need a second person who checks the record rather than the email? And are SPF, DKIM and DMARC published for every domain you own, including ones that send no mail, with a reject policy once your own mail passes and someone reading the reports? If you run phishing simulations, get written scope and consent from leadership first, tell staff a programme exists, include requests with no link, make reporting one click, and never name or shame. Standards: if your company is pursuing ISO/IEC 27001:2022, this is Annex A 6.3 (information security awareness, education and training) and A.5.14 (information transfer); if your SOC 2 report is in scope, CC2.2 (communicating information security responsibilities internally) applies; NIST SP 800-50 Rev. 1 describes the learning programme. A payment process where one person can redirect money is a finding an auditor is likely to raise, so build the call back and the second approver into the first design rather than at audit time.

recall.prompt: A long-standing supplier emails your accounts team from its usual address: its bank has changed, and next week's invoice should go to the new account. Your mail program shows SPF, DKIM and DMARC all passing. What do you do, and what rule would you set?

keyIdeas.idea: Passing checks show the mail came from the supplier's own domain, not that the request is genuine; the supplier's mailbox may have been broken into
Confirm by phone on a number already on file, never one from the email
A second person checks the account against the supplier record before any payment

recall.model: Don't pay or change anything yet. The checks only prove the message came from servers the supplier's domain allows and wasn't changed on the way, not that the request is genuine: a real mailbox that has been broken into passes all three. Look up the supplier's phone number in your own records, the number on file, and call them to ask whether their bank details really changed; never use a number from the email. Only then update the record. Set the rule for everyone, with no exceptions for urgent requests: every change of bank details is confirmed by a call back, and every payment needs a second person who checks the account against the supplier record before approving.

recall.prompt: An email passes SPF, DKIM and DMARC. What does that show?
options: It came from servers the domain after the @ allows, and wasn't changed on the way
The sender is the person named in the display name
The domain is the organisation you think it is
The request in it is genuine
recall.why: All three check the domain the message shows. A lookalike domain is its own domain and passes for itself; the display name and the request aren't checked at all.

recall.prompt: In the sim, which of these stops £8,640 going to the new account?
options: DMARC set to reject on the charity's domain
A banner on mail from outside the domain
recall.why: The second person compares the account with the supplier file and won't approve, so the payment is held. The checks, the banner and a link test leave it paid: the lookalike passes for itself, and the request had no link.

recall.prompt: Your manager wants to send the finance team practice phishing emails next month and retrain whoever clicks. How would you run it fairly, and what would you measure?

keyIdeas.idea: Written scope and consent from leadership first, and staff told a programme exists
Make reporting safe and easy, and count reports, not only clicks
No shaming or punishment; results improve training and processes

recall.model: Start with written scope agreed and signed off by leadership: what is sent, to whom, when, and what is never imitated, with consent at the organisation level and staff told that a programme exists. Include requests with no link, such as a change of bank details, because those are what cost money. Give everyone a one-click report button and thank every report. Measure the reporting rate and time to report, not only clicks. Use results to improve training and processes, never shame anyone or punish a click, because fear makes people hide mistakes and slows the reports you need.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 3 months later. The rule has held: every change of bank details waits for a phone call. On Monday 11 January 2027 a letter came by post on what looked like Harcastle's letterhead: new bank details, and a new phone number for queries. On Tuesday 12 January Mr Tuckwell rang the number printed in the letter; a polite man confirmed everything. He updated Harcastle's record and, on Thursday 14 January, paid invoice 1240, £2,310. On Friday 15 January Harcastle rang to ask where its money was.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. The phone call happened, so why didn't it stop the payment, and what should change?

keyIdeas.idea: The number came from the request itself, so the call reached the fraudster, not Harcastle
Ring the number already held in the supplier file from before the request
Changes to the supplier record itself need a second person and the same check

coldCase.model: The call proved nothing, because the number came from the request itself: the number printed in the letter was the fraudster's, so a call to it reached the fraudster and confirmed his own story. A call back only works on a number you held before the request arrived. Ring the number on file in the supplier file, the office number Harcastle has had there since 2019, and ignore any number in the letter. And guard the record itself: changes to the record, a bank account or a phone number, need a second person and the same call on the old number, so a letter can't swap the number you would call.
